title: Emergency Presentation of Cancer Common in Older Adults
summary: A national Medicare study of 929,378 older US adults found 28% of cancer diagnoses were emergency presentations (EPs). EP prevalence and mortality varied by cancer type, with inpatient EPs showing markedly higher 30-day and one-year mortality even after adjusting for age, stage, comorbidity, and frailty.
content:
HealthDay News — Emergency presentation (EP) for cancer diagnosis is common among older US adults and predicts persistently elevated mortality, according to a study published online July 14 in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute.

Caroline A. Thompson, PhD, from University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, and colleagues estimated EP prevalence and associated mortality across cancer types in a national Medicare cohort. The analysis included 929,378 patients with 16 high-burden cancers diagnosed from 2008 to 2017.

The researchers found that 28% were EPs (22% inpatient, 6% outpatient). Prevalence of EP varied across cancer type from less than 10% for breast and prostate cancer to greater than 40% for liver, lung, stomach, colon, ovarian, and pancreatic cancers. For non-EPs, one-year survival was 81% vs 60% for outpatient EPs and 36% for inpatient EPs. Inpatient EPs had nearly fourfold higher 30-day adjusted mortality than non-EPs (risk ratio [RR], 3.88; ranging from 2.1 for pancreatic cancer to 6.3 for lymphoma). Inpatient EPs with 90-day survival had 51% higher one-year mortality (RR, 1.51; ranging from 1.1 for pancreatic cancer to 2.1 for lymphoma). Intermediate risk was seen for outpatient EPs (one-year mortality RR, 1.28).

"These gaps held up even after we accounted for age, cancer stage, other illnesses, and frailty," Thompson said in a statement. "How a cancer is found carries information about a patient’s outlook that goes beyond the tumor itself."

One author disclosed financial ties to the biopharmaceutical industry.
